title: Joining Sidney Bechet's quartet at Jimmy Ryan's
summary: At Jimmy Ryan's across from the Three Deuces, Bechet takes Leeman with Kenny Kersey and Vic Dickenson; he was strict with drummers but seemed pleased.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: On 52nd Street, I worked the other side of the coin, as they say. I went into the so-called Dixieland oriented club of Jimmy Ryan's across the street from the Three Deuces. I hadn't known Sidney previously, I believe Jimmy Ryan himself asked me or recommended me to Sidney, and Sidney asked if I'd go in with him with a quartet, the wonderful Kenny Kersey on piano and Vic Dickenson on trombone, and myself.
I consider myself lucky to have the ability to go from a Webster oriented group to work with and please a traditional New Orleans legend.

Sidney Bechet was very strict with drummers, he had that reputation, I'd heard that from Zutty, and the time had to go exactly his way. He was rather gruff and rather hard to get close to. But once Kenny Kersey and I got the feel of the thing, he seemed pleased and I never had any serious words with him. He seemed very pleased with what we did for him. There was a Bechet album issued in France the last few years -- 2 or 3 years ago, and it's a long playing album, three playing sides, three long playing records, I mean -- let me get this straight now -- an LP,
